figures.shows: Illustration of support vector data description: input space (left) with a curved nominal cluster of blue points and scattered orange anomalies; feature space (right) with the nominal points enclosed in a small hypersphere on a sphere and anomalies outside. No numeric axes.
figures.confirmed_by: Input data are mapped into a higher-dimensional feature space, where the nominal samples are enclosed by a minimum-volume hypersphere

figures.shows: Quantum kernel evaluation circuit: U_phi(x) then U_phi dagger(x prime) on n qubits initialised in |0>, all qubits measured to a classical register; the pairwise return probabilities fill the Gram matrix K, which goes to the classical anomaly detection solver.
figures.confirmed_by: is estimated as the return probability of the all-zero bitstring.

figures.shows: Four-panel schematic of sources of exponential concentration: (a) expressivity, (b) global measurements, (c) entanglement, (d) noise. No numeric axes.
figures.confirmed_by: Illustration of the four primary mechanisms associated with exponential concentration in quantum kernels

figures.shows: Angle-encoding feature map circuit: one RX(x_i) gate per qubit, then RX dagger(x prime_i), measurement of all qubits; no entangling gates.
figures.confirmed_by: No entangling gates are applied, such that each feature is encoded independently.

figures.shows: (a) Three-qubit Full ZZ feature map: Hadamard, phase gates P(2 x_i) and CNOT-phase-CNOT pairwise interactions. (b) ZZ-R map: Full ZZ block repeated three times with fixed random layers between. (c) Fixed random layer: RZ-RY-RZ rotations plus nearest-neighbor CNOTs.
figures.confirmed_by: in which the Full ZZ encoding is repeated three times with fixed random unitary layers

figures.shows: Two panels against feature dimension d (number of qubits, 1 to 20) for four kernels (ae, zz, zz_reuploading, rbf), 500 training samples, mean over 12 seeds, shaded band one standard deviation. (a) mean off-diagonal kernel value (0 to 1) falls for all four kernels; at 20 qubits about 0.45 (ae), about 0.39 (zz_reuploading), about 0.17 (rbf), about 0.13 (zz). (b) off-diagonal variance on a log axis; zz peaks at about 6 qubits then falls to about 0.004 at 20; the others sit near 0.02 to 0.03 at 20 qubits.
figures.confirmed_by: Across this range, the median off-diagonal fidelity decreases from 0.998 at one qubit to 0.458 at 20 qubits

figures.shows: Fidelity Gram matrices (diagonal masked, colour bar 0 to about 0.8, capped at p99) of the 20-qubit angle-encoding, ZZ and ZZ re-uploading kernels from the same 500-sample training set (seed 1). The ZZ matrix is mostly dark (low values); the other two are brighter.
figures.confirmed_by: The three matrices illustrate the distinct kernel geometries produced by the evaluated feature maps

figures.shows: One-class SVM schematic in a two-dimensional plane (x1, x2 from 0 to 5): a straight hyperplane boundary w.phi(x)=rho separates blue inliers (upper right) from red outliers (lower left), with the normal vector w drawn.
figures.confirmed_by: A hyperplane decision boundary w · ϕ(x) = ρ separates the normal (inlier) region from anomalous (outlier) regions in the feature space.

figures.shows: Support vector regression schematic: x from 0 to 5, y from about -1 to 1; data points as crosses, a fitted sine-like SVR curve and a shaded epsilon-insensitive tube.
figures.confirmed_by: Predictions within an ε-insensitive tube of the regression function incur no loss

figures.shows: Classical kernels: linear k = x^T x prime (feature-space dimension n, vector alignment), polynomial (x^T x prime + c)^d (dimension n+d choose d, higher-order feature interactions), Gaussian RBF exp(-gamma norm^2) (infinite dimension, distance-based similarity).
figures.confirmed_by: Examples of classical kernels, their feature-space dimensionality, and their similarity interpretations.

figures.shows: Mean AP (12 seeds, 20 PCA components) for eight kernel-detector configurations at 500, 1,000, 2,000 and 4,000 training samples and the AP gain from 500 to 4,000 (0.041 to 0.057).
figures.confirmed_by: Average precision (12 seeds, 20 PCA components) as training-set size grows under cluster downsampling.

figures.shows: Fitted power-law parameters A, B, alpha, thresholds N*(0.001) and N*(0.0001), slope at 4,000 and R squared for each of the eight configurations; A from 0.8250 to 0.8670, alpha from 0.4176 to 0.8083.
figures.confirmed_by: All configurations exhibit sublinear convergence toward the fitted asymptote (0 < α < 1).

figures.shows: AP at 500 samples, fitted asymptote A, gap from A (6.81 to 10.21 percent) and performance retained (89.79 to 93.19 percent) for the eight configurations.
figures.confirmed_by: Across the evaluated kernel-detector configurations, 500 training samples retain 89.79–93.19% of the fitted asymptotic AP.

figures.shows: Off-diagonal mean, median (p50) and variance at 20 qubits for angle encoding, ZZ and ZZ re-uploading (12 seeds).
figures.confirmed_by: Off-diagonal kernel statistics at the 20-qubit operating point.

figures.shows: AP for AE, ZZ-R, RBF and ZZ kernels with OC-SVM and QSVR at 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200 and 350 landmarks and for the exact 500-sample kernel.

papers.what_it_is: An experimental paper that trains quantum image classifiers by classical simulation on the Honda Scenes data and runs inference on Quantinuum H1/H2 and IBM Brisbane/Fez, with up to 72 qubits and over 3000 two-qubit gates.

existing.note: Confirmed. Table 1 (p.7) gives the numbers: the 0.94 BAE model has 3652 parameters; the CNN with 1994 parameters scores 0.97 and the fully-connected network with 8196 parameters scores 0.93. papers.what_it_is: A method and hardware-test paper that extends hierarchical QCBM training to load MNIST and Honda Scenes images (up to 21 qubits, and block amplitude encoding to 72 qubits) and runs coarse-grained checks on IBM and Quantinuum devices.

existing.note: Narrowed. The 21-qubit hardware run is the IBM Algiers naive-loading circuit (229 gates, 80 two-qubit gates), checked only through single-qubit Z expectation values and the joint distribution over the 3 most significant bits, not the full loaded image. The "10 qubit circuits for MNIST" compares with the 10-qubit MNIST circuits of this paper and of the cited MNISQ library.
existing.value: The authors report that their methods train and implement image loading on 21 qubit circuits on existing quantum hardware, compared to 10 qubit circuits for MNIST, with the hardware result checked only on coarse-grained statistics of the most significant qubits.
quotes: Our methods allow us to train and implement image loading on 21 qubit circuits on existing quantum hardware, compared to the 10 qubit circuits for MNIST.
For the full naive loading of the image, we probe the joint distribution over the first 3 most significant bits.

existing.note: Confirmed as the authors belief. The paper reports no gradient-magnitude measurement; the supporting data are the KL divergence comparison of Figure 3 (0.034 hierarchical against 0.042 non-hierarchical at 21 qubits, with the parameter count stated as 1100 in the text and 1000 in the figure title).
quotes: Ultimately, we believe the hierarchical ansatz is an effective strategy for avoiding barren plateaus

existing.note: Confirmed. The paper gives two reasons: too few shots for a distribution over 2 to the power 21 points, and measurement and readout errors on all qubits.

existing.note: Narrowed. The paper gives no numerical fidelity for this comparison; the evidence is the visual comparison in Figure 2 of 9 digits. The compared F80 library has a threshold fidelity of 80% and at most 65 two-qubit gates, defines fidelity as the overlap |<psi|phi>| (not squared, footnote 1), and encodes image data in the absolute value of the amplitudes, while this paper encodes it in the square of the amplitudes (Figure 2 caption).

we encode the image data in the square of the amplitudes while the MNISQ dataset encodes the image data in the absolute value of the wave function amplitudes.
